newsitem.title: USA: Democrats set to return more questionable funds.
newsitem.headline: Democrats set to return more questionable funds.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's Democratic Party, battered by revelations of fund-raising improprieties, planned on Friday to return a reported $1.5 million in questionable donations.

The Democratic National Committee, the fund-raising and administrative arm of the party, scheduled a 1:30 p.m. EST (1830 GMT) news conference to make public an internal audit of its fund-raising activities by a law firm and accounting company hired by the party.

As a result of the audit, party sources said, more funds would be returned. But a party official refused to confirm or deny a Washington Post report that disputed funds totaling nearly $1.5 million, "mostly from Asian Americans," would be returned because of questions about their sources.
That would more than double the $1.47 million the party already announced had been returned because of questions about whether the money was given illegally.

The uproar over fund raising has included ethical and legal questions about the invitations to big contributors for overnight stays in the Lincoln bedroom of the White House as well as coffee chats and golf outings with Clinton. The president has denied that the invitations to hundreds of friends and contributors broke any laws.

Four investigations into financing activities are under way, including whether the governments of China or other countries attempted to influence U.S. policy. A federal grand jury probing the issue under the direction of a Justice Department task force heard testimony on Friday from a woman who refused to identify herself to reporters afterwards.
Committees from the House of Representatives, the Senate and the Federal Election Commission are investigating reports of wrongdoing in the 1996 election campaign.

Among gifts already returned was $450,000 from an Indonesian couple living in Virginia who were reportedly recruited for donations by John Huang, a one-time Commerce Department official and former Democratic fund-raiser.

The party said it would refund the money to Arief and Soraya Wiriadinata when the source was questioned. Huang, a key figure in various probes, was the top American executive of the Indonesia-based Lippo Group financial conglomerate before going to the Commerce Department in 1994.

Only Americans or foreign nationals living legally in the country can donate to campaigns. U.S. corporations or foreign companies with U.S. subsidiaries doing substantial business here can donate unlimited amounts of "soft money" to political parties for party building and get-out-the vote activities.

The controversy over improper fund raising follows the most expensive U.S. election ever. The Federal Election Commission estimated almost $2.7 billion was spent on 1996 presidential and congressional races.
But the publicity about fund raising apparently is having an impact on donors who dislike questions about their giving.

"It's a little uneasy when you give a donation, you're susddenly barraged by press calls," Democratic Party spokeswoman Amy Weiss Tobe said. "There are a lot of people who think 'If I write a check, am I going to get a call from every wire and newspaper in this country?'"
